results.title: Clip
results.note: Keeps the parts of the countries that fall inside the rectangle. One country stays one feature, and only the countries’ own attributes come through.

results.title: Erase
results.note: The opposite of clip: everything the rectangle covers is cut away. Ireland disappears entirely, because the rectangle contains all of it.

results.title: Intersect
results.note: The same geometry as clip, but one feature per overlapping pair — and the rectangle’s attributes travel with it. Its `name` collides with the countries’ `name`, so it arrives as `name_2`.

results.title: Union (overlay)
results.note: Every piece of both layers: the overlap, the countries outside the rectangle, and the rectangle outside the countries. `part` says which of the three a feature is, and a piece with no counterpart has NULL where the other layer’s fields would be.

result.name: gp_result
warnings: 1 result had no geometry left and were dropped — either the operation removed everything, or that shape could not be calculated.

results.title: Select by location — touch or overlap
results.note: Keeps whole features that touch the rectangle at all. Geometry is untouched — this filters, it does not cut.

results.title: Select by location — lie completely inside
results.note: Stricter: only Ireland qualifies, because the United Kingdom sticks out of the rectangle.

results.title: Select by location — do not touch
results.note: The negation: the three mainland countries, which the rectangle never reaches.

results.title: Spatial join — touches or overlaps
results.note: Every country keeps its own geometry and gains the rectangle’s attributes where the two meet. Countries that do not meet it keep their geometry and get nothing.

results.title: Spatial join — lies inside
results.note: Only a country that lies entirely within the rectangle picks up its attributes.

results.title: Spatial join — contains
results.note: The mirror image: the country would have to contain the rectangle. None does, so nothing is matched — the same layer back, with empty columns.

results.title: Dissolve
results.note: Merges features that share a value and removes the boundaries between them — here the `eu` attribute, so the four members become one shape and the United Kingdom stays its own. The members are not all adjacent, so their shape is one feature in several pieces: Ireland is an island, and dissolving does not pretend otherwise. Leave the grouping empty to merge the whole layer into one.

results.title: Statistics
results.note: The same grouping as dissolve, without the geometry: a table rather than a layer. Nothing is drawn, which is the point — no expensive geometry work when the answer is a count.

results.title: Centroid
results.note: One point per feature, at its centre of area. A centroid can fall outside its own shape — a crescent’s does — which is what the label point is for.

results.title: Label point
results.note: One point per feature, guaranteed *inside* it and as far from the edges as possible. Where you would put the name.

results.title: Buffer
results.note: A zone at a fixed distance on the ground — 50 km here. Measured in metres, not degrees, so it is the same width at every latitude.

results.title: Convex hull
results.note: The smallest shape with no dents that still contains everything — an elastic band round the layer.

results.title: Simplify
results.note: Fewer points, same map. A shared border is simplified once and both neighbours keep identical points, so no slivers open up between them.

results.title: Cartogram
results.note: Each country resized so its *area* shows its population rather than its ground area: Ireland shrinks, the United Kingdom and France grow. The default method stretches one sheet, so neighbours stay attached — Belgium and the Netherlands do not come apart, and no gaps open along the borders.

results.title: Voronoi
results.note: Defined on points: one cell per point, covering everything closer to it than to any other. Hand it polygons or lines and each feature is first reduced to one point — a polygon’s area centroid, or the point halfway along a line — and the cells are built from those, so a layer of countries gives one cell per country.

results.title: Delaunay
results.note: The mirror image of Voronoi, and defined on points in the same way: triangles joining the points that are neighbours. A polygon or line input is reduced to one point per feature first — a polygon’s area centroid, or the point halfway along a line — and the triangles join those. Every input point ends up a corner of at least one triangle, which is why the distinct corners number exactly as many as the inputs. It is not merely a step towards Voronoi: a triangulation is the usual way to turn spot heights into a terrain surface (a TIN, and the contours and slopes read off it), to interpolate between measurements, and to ask which points are neighbours without choosing a distance — the neighbour graph spatial statistics builds its weights from. What comes back here is only the triangles and the indices of the points at their corners, with no attributes carried over and no height, so in this tool it answers the neighbour-and-spacing question rather than the surface one.
